scope: Illumina ATAC-Seq explanatory schematic and the explicitly cited adaptations, at the shared molecular-architecture level. The graph extracts the unbranched depicted route from native chromatin through Tn5 tagmentation and the combined DNA purification/amplification block to a DNA library. The initial assay overview and repeated "Open DNA" panel illustrate the same accessibility target, without a depicted chromatin-opening operation. Blue Tn5 icons bearing colored adapter marks are reagents; insertion and "Fragmented and primed" depict one coupled transformation. The drawing contains no cell-isolation, compartment-pooling, barcode-assignment or sequencing operation. Named adaptations are qualified in method_scopes rather than expanded into unshown workflows. The two single-cell references describe distinct implementations, not interchangeable names for the same cell-handling architecture. THS-seq is a cited comparator, not a depicted ATAC-seq variant.

states.label: Native chromatin with exposed DNA ("Open DNA")
features: Genomic DNA is packaged with gray nucleosome icons and exposed between them; the far-left assay overview highlights an exposed segment in yellow.
"Open DNA" denotes accessible DNA within native chromatin. The original ATAC-seq implementation acts on unfixed nuclei; it is not a naked-DNA accessibility assay.
No cell-identity barcode or compartment boundary is specified in the Illumina drawing.

states.label: Purified, amplified DNA library (terminal "DNA")
features: Terminal parallel linear DNA fragments carry colored adapter end marks and are labelled "DNA"; nucleosome icons are absent from the final product panel.
This is a DNA sequencing library. Genomic DNA inserts and their insertion boundaries carry the accessibility information into sequencing; no RNA intermediate or protein readout is depicted.

The card describes deep sequencing as the downstream readout. In the primary implementation, mapped insertion positions locate preferentially accessible chromatin, while paired-end insert lengths support inference of nucleosome organization.
Footprint patterns can support inference of DNA-binding-protein occupancy, as shown by the primary paper; protein identity and occupancy are not directly read as a sequenced protein molecule.

Recovery is selective: PCR-compatible adapter pairing and spacing affect which transposition products enter the amplified library. The card also warns that sample processing can expose previously bound chromatin.

operations.label: Insert in regions of open chromatin → Fragmented and primed
operations.description: Adapter-loaded Tn5 transposomes act on accessible portions of native chromatin DNA, simultaneously fragmenting it and inserting sequencing-adapter tags. The central insertion panel and the arrow to "Fragmented and primed" show reagent action and its product within this single coupled transformation; no prior chromatin-opening reaction is drawn.
operations.mechanism: Tn5 transposase delivers its adapter payload to chromatin DNA. Steric hindrance makes transposition less probable in less accessible chromatin, so tagging is preferential rather than perfectly exclusive. The blue enzyme icon denotes the catalytic reagent; it is not an additional biological analyte or a separate workflow operation.
operations.information_effect: Genomic sequence, insertion boundaries and distances between insertion events encode a sample of accessibility in the original chromatin. Protection by nucleosomes or bound proteins can alter this fragmentation pattern, allowing subsequent inference rather than direct sequencing of those proteins.

operations.label: DNA purification / Amplification
operations.description: The "Fragmented and primed" material passes through the depicted combined DNA purification/amplification block, producing purified, amplified linear DNA library fragments. Purification recovers tagged DNA, and PCR increases the abundance of amplifiable fragments. The graph retains this as one broad operation rather than reconstructing internal cleanup steps.
operations.mechanism: PCR copies fragments carrying compatible sequencing-adapter sites. The original bulk ATAC-seq protocol explicitly describes purification after transposition followed by PCR; this block is a schematic abstraction, not a fixed cleanup order for every input or named adaptation.
operations.information_effect: The amplified genomic inserts retain their origin and insertion-boundary information, enabling sequence-based mapping of accessible regions. Amplification filters the tagged population by adapter compatibility and spacing; read recovery does not imply perfect accessibility specificity or recovery of every insertion event.

method_scopes.rationale: ATAC-seq is the named core method; ATAC-Seq capitalization and the expanded Assay for Transposase Accessible Chromatin using sequencing are aliases. Both graph operations apply at figure scope. The primary paper establishes native chromatin tagmentation followed by PCR, and supports insertion-position, insert-length and footprint readouts. The figure does not show nuclei preparation or sequencing. Its combined purification/amplification block does not require pre-PCR purification in every low-input implementation; the original paper expressly omits that cleanup in its low-cell-number version.

method_scopes.method: ATAC-seq on cryopreserved iPSC-derived motor neurons
method_scopes.rationale: The Milani paper describes a sample-preservation adaptation of ATAC-seq, not a new assay alias. Slow-cooled cryopreservation of the tested iPSC-derived motor neurons preserves usable nuclei, whereas flash-freezing failed in that comparison. Tagmentation, DNA purification and PCR map to the graph at its broad level. This implementation additionally selects nucleosome-free fragments for single-end sequencing; the generic library state is therefore not a claim that its sequenced size distribution equals the original paired-end ATAC library. Preservation and size selection are paper-supported scope distinctions, not extra operations drawn by Illumina.

method_scopes.method: single-cell ATAC-seq by combinatorial cellular indexing
method_scopes.rationale: The card’s single-cell ATAC-seq citation is Cusanovich 2015, a distinct combinatorial cellular-indexing implementation. Adapter-loaded transposase tagging maps to op_tagment, using barcoded transposase complexes in this implementation. Populations of intact nuclei are first tagged, then intact nuclei are pooled and redistributed; nuclei are subsequently lysed and a second barcode is added by PCR. PCR products are pooled for sequencing. This preserves nucleus-to-fragment association through a combination of indexes, with possible barcode collisions. The main text supports PCR but does not establish a full match to the figure’s combined purification/amplification block, so op_library is not assigned wholesale. These unshown compartment/indexing operations do not become branches of the Illumina graph. The unresolved point is whole-block applicability, not the established tagmentation or indexed-PCR transformations.

evidence.locator: Main text, combinatorial indexing architecture, [b00005]
evidence.quote: First, we molecularly barcode populations of nuclei in each of many wells. We then pool, dilute and redistribute intact nuclei to a second set of wells, introduce a second barcode and complete library construction.

evidence.locator: Main text, integrated method and Fig. 1A reference, [b00007]
evidence.quote: After lysing nuclei, a second barcode is introduced during PCR with indexed primers complementary to the transposase-introduced adapters. Finally, all PCR products are pooled and sequenced, with the expectation that most sequence reads bearing the same combination of barcodes will be derived from a single cell

evidence.locator: Main text, combinatorial indexing architecture, [b00005]
evidence.quote: The rate of “collisions”, i.e. nuclei coincidentally receiving the same combination of indexes, can be tuned by adjusting how many nuclei are distributed to the second set of wells (Fig. S1; (19)).

evidence.locator: Retrieved PubMed publication metadata: PMID and title
evidence.quote: "title": "Characterization of chromatin accessibility with a transposome hypersensitive sites sequencing (THS-seq) assay.",
evidence.rationale: The paper actually describes THS-seq and compares it with ATAC-seq. Illumina cites it for ATAC adapter-orientation and spacing limitations. This background comparison does not make THS-seq an ATAC-seq alias or import its T7/transcription chemistry into the figure-derived architecture.

evidence.locator: Results and discussion, THS-seq design and implementation, [b00010]
evidence.quote: First, the Tn5 transposome complex inserts adaptors in random orientation, such that only half of the molecules contain the adaptors in the orientation required for PCR amplification. Second, only approximately 1 % of the genome is accessible in typical cells, and the regions in which two adjacent transposition events are too far apart cannot be amplified by PCR.
evidence.rationale: This is the cited THS-seq paper’s account of limitations in the ATAC-seq design it compares against; the half-molecule statement is not a universal measured yield for every ATAC variant.

evidence.locator: Results and discussion, THS-seq design and implementation, [b00010]
evidence.quote: We therefore developed the THS-seq method, which uses a customized Tn5 transposome system to attach a T7 promoter [22–25] to the end of every DNA molecule after in vitro transposition.
evidence.rationale: THS-seq is the distinct method described by this paper. Its T7-promoter/linear-transcription library architecture is not shown in the Illumina ATAC-seq figure and is not imported into this graph.
